chapter: First Blue Note recording with Jackie McLean
title: Rehearsal at Lynn Oliver's studio and the Blue Note session with Haynes and Hancock
summary: Rehearsal with Alfred Lion and Frank Wolff, the Empire Hotel and cab ride to Van Gelder's, and praise for the Haynes and Hancock interplay on his debut.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: And he says, “Do you have any tunes?” I said, “Yes I do.” He says, “Let me hear them, let me play them.” He says, “Okay I’m putting you on my next record date.” Now I’ve told that story many times and every time people said you’ve got to be kidding. He hadn’t heard you yet. I said, “Well he was going on what Jim Harrison said, ‘Hey you know there’s a new trumpet player in town.’” You know. Boom. And so, and then to get on that, there was a place called Len Oliver’s Studio, it was a famous place on 89th and Broadway where most rehearsals went down. And that’s what Alfred Lion used for rehearsing bands before taking them to Rudy Van Gelder’s. And I arrived for the first day’s rehearsal, I did not know who Jackie McLean was having on his record date. I just knew wow, I’m going to be on my first record date. And I get to the studio and Alfred and Frank Wolff, his beloved partner is there. And I looked at the drums and there’s Roy Haynes sitting on the drums so I’m already, oh man. And then you know, in walks Herbie Hancock you know, on the piano. The only new person, new persons, was me and Cecil McBee. That’s his first time out. And Alfred starts his stopwatch, we go through the tunes, and there’s this famous hotel, it’s still there, the Empire Hotel was the meeting place. That’s where every one of those great recordings of Blue Note started. The old Checker Cab would be waiting in front of the hotel with a box full of sandwiches and beer, soda, liquor. We all pile in those Checker Cabs and off to Rudy Van Gelder’s across the George Washington Bridge we’d go. And that first recording, I still think that’s one of the best recordings of Jackie and all of us on there. Because it was, as we started this conversation, it was loose and free but at the same time cohesive with the modern bebop jazz element as well. And the interplay between Roy Haynes and Herbie Hancock is just absolutely miraculous. I mean it’s one of the greatest performances by those two together ever, and the only time they’ve ever been commercially recorded you know, for a label. So that particular record, not only being my debut record, it’s a substantial contribution.
